metadata.summary: This practice guidance reviews the epidemiology, physiology, risk factors, and types of hypersensitivity reactions to iodinated and gadolinium-based contrast media. It evaluates evidence for premedication protocols and allergy investigations, and provides consensus recommendations to inform hospital policies and reduce breakthrough reactions.

conditions_covered: Hypersensitivity reactions to iodinated contrast media
Hypersensitivity reactions to gadolinium-based contrast agents
target_population: Patients with history of contrast media hypersensitivity

conditions.name: Hypersensitivity Reaction to Contrast Media
conditions.description: Adverse immune-mediated responses to iodinated contrast media or gadolinium-based contrast agents following intravenous injection, presenting along a spectrum from mild urticaria to life-threatening anaphylaxis. These reactions are triggered by the contrast molecule itself, not by iodine.
conditions.epidemiology: Immediate hypersensitivity reactions to low osmolar contrast media arise in approximately 0.38% of administrations, with severe events in 0.02%; delayed reactions occur in 0.05%. For gadolinium-based contrast agents, hypersensitivity reactions are documented in less than 0.4% of uses, and anaphylaxis rates range from 0.00003% to 0.004%. Key risk factors include a prior hypersensitivity reaction to contrast media, atopic history, female sex, and higher contrast concentration or injection rate.
conditions.clinical_presentation: Immediate reactions (within 1 hour) manifest as urticaria, angioedema, bronchospasm, hypotension, or anaphylaxis. Delayed reactions (hours to days later) usually present as maculopapular exanthema, with rare severe cutaneous adverse events such as acute generalized exanthematous pustulosis, drug reaction with eosinophilia and systemic symptoms, or Stevens–Johnson syndrome/toxic epidermal necrolysis.

subtypes.name: Immediate Hypersensitivity Reaction
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Develops within 1 hour of contrast administration; can be IgE-mediated or non-IgE-mediated; may progress to anaphylaxis with cardiovascular compromise.

subtypes.name: Delayed Hypersensitivity Reaction
subtypes.distinguishing_features: Appears hours to days after exposure; predominantly T-cell driven; usually mild skin eruptions but occasionally severe systemic reactions.

diagnostic_workup.purpose: Identify the responsible contrast agent and assess cross-reactivity among agents
diagnostic_workup.when_indicated: After a severe hypersensitivity reaction to guide selection of a safe alternative contrast medium
diagnostic_workup.interpretation: Cross-reactivity on skin testing correlates with shared side chains between iodinated contrast media; choosing an agent with a different side chain lowers the risk of recurrence.

staging.system: American College of Radiology severity classification (mild, moderate, severe)
staging.additional_rules: Detailed definitions appear in Appendix A of the source guideline (not included in the present extraction).

toxicities.incidence: Acute HR rates: LOCM ~0.4%–3.13%, GBCA ~0.4% (overall), macrocyclic GBCA 14/10,000, linear ionic 8.3/10,000, linear nonionic 1.5/10,000. Breakthrough rates: same ICM without premedication 15%, with premedication 19%, different ICM 3% (McDonald 2021); same GBCA without premedication 31.4%, with premedication 19.0%, different GBCA without premedication 6.0%, with premedication 4.8% (Ahn 2022).
recognition: Urticaria, pruritus, cutaneous edema, nasal congestion, sneezing, conjunctivitis, rhinorrhea
Throat tightness, hoarseness, wheezing, bronchospasm, hypoxia
Delayed reactions: maculopapular exanthem, SJS/TEN, DRESS, AGEP
toxicities.grading: ACR categories: Mild (self-limited, no treatment needed), Moderate (require medical management, some may progress), Severe (life-threatening, may cause permanent morbidity or death)
prevention: Contrast agent switching is effective in reducing recurrent reactions.
Routine premedication with corticosteroids and/or antihistamines is not recommended; evidence is weak and potential harms exist.
For severe index reactions (e.g., anaphylaxis, SJS/TEN, DRESS), consider allergy consultation and skin/intradermal testing for alternative agents.

toxicities.event: Adverse effects of premedication (corticosteroids and antihistamines)
toxicities.incidence: Projected harms per prevented contrast-related death: 551 hospital-acquired infections, 32 infection-related deaths. NNT to prevent one lethal reaction: 56,900 (95% CI 38,900–108,300). Short-term oral corticosteroid risks: avascular necrosis RR 1.60 (95% CI 1.34–1.84), bone fracture in children OR 1.17 (95% CI 1.04–1.33). Pediatric corticosteroid course (<14 days) may cause vomiting, behavioral changes, mood swings, sleep disturbance, and infections.
recognition: First-generation antihistamines: sedation, poor sleep quality, cardiac toxicity, respiratory depression, coma, death.
Corticosteroids: hyperglycemia, insomnia, mood disturbances, avascular necrosis, infections, fractures, venous thromboembolism.
prevention: CSACI recommends using second/third-generation antihistamines over first-generation agents.
Avoid routine corticosteroid premedication; balance potential benefits against risks.
Consider an accelerated 5-hour IV corticosteroid regimen if urgent premedication is deemed necessary (non-inferior to 13-hour oral protocol but does not eliminate all moderate/severe reactions).

prophylaxis.recommendation: Routine premedication with corticosteroids and/or antihistamines is not recommended due to insufficient evidence and potential harms. Switching to a structurally different contrast agent is the preferred strategy to reduce breakthrough reactions. For patients with severe prior reactions (e.g., anaphylaxis, SJS/TEN, DRESS), allergy consultation and skin testing may guide selection of an alternative agent.
prophylaxis.target_population: Patients with a history of hypersensitivity reaction to contrast media

recommendations.statement: The exact dose and specific name of any contrast medium must be recorded in the patient's electronic health record for easy retrieval in case of a hypersensitivity reaction. Following an acute reaction, the culprit agent's name must be documented in the radiology report, which is sent to the referring clinician and archived in PACS. Additionally, the timing, characteristics, and management of the reaction should be documented. A system for reporting delayed hypersensitivity reactions should be established.
recommendations.rationale: Proper documentation ensures that the offending agent can be identified and avoided in future examinations, facilitating contrast switching.

recommendations.statement: The sole risk factor for a future hypersensitivity reaction is a prior hypersensitivity reaction to the identical type of contrast medium (i.e., LOCM ICM or GBCA). No other risk factors warrant routine screening. Clinicians must differentiate between true hypersensitivity and physiologic reactions.
recommendations.rationale: Evidence indicates that only previous HR to the same contrast type consistently predicts future reactions; screening other purported risk factors is not evidence-based.

recommendations.statement: In patients with any severity of prior hypersensitivity reaction to ICM or GBCA, administering a chemically distinct contrast agent is the most effective strategy to prevent a recurrent reaction. If a mild or moderate breakthrough reaction occurs despite switching, a third agent should be used. Institutions must maintain at least two different contrast agents; sole-supplier contracts should permit procurement of an alternative agent.
recommendations.rationale: Studies show that contrast switching significantly reduces breakthrough reaction rates compared to re-challenge with the same agent.

recommendations.statement: When the culprit ICM is unknown, management depends on the timing and severity of the antecedent reaction. If the reaction occurred before 2000, the agent was likely not low-osmolality, and current LOCM can be administered without premedication. For reactions on or after 2000: if severe, consider an alternative imaging modality or allergy consultation; premedication is not advised. If mild or moderate, premedication with second-generation antihistamines and close monitoring is suggested.
recommendations.rationale: Prior to 2000, high-osmolality contrast media were commonly used; reactions to those agents are not predictive of reactions to modern low-osmolality agents.

recommendations.statement: Steroid premedication for patients with a prior hypersensitivity reaction to LOCM is not justified by high-quality evidence; existing studies are methodologically weak and involved HOCM. Given the lack of efficacy and potential harms, the routine use of corticosteroids for prophylaxis in high-risk patients is discouraged and should be abandoned.
recommendations.rationale: No robust evidence supports corticosteroid premedication for LOCM; historic data on HOCM are not applicable, and steroids carry risks of adverse effects and increased hospitalization.

recommendations.statement: For patients with a previous hypersensitivity reaction to GBCA, corticosteroid premedication is not advised. The evidence is conflicting, but the net benefit is minimal and potential harms exist.

Second-generation antihistamines may reduce breakthrough reactions in patients with a history of mild hypersensitivity. Their additional benefit after contrast switching is uncertain and may be considered optional. Oral second-generation antihistamines should be administered at least 1 hour before contrast injection.

There is currently inadequate evidence to prefer any specific LOCM product for reducing hypersensitivity reactions. Although preliminary data suggest that the choice of agent for contrast switching might be based on molecular structure, this evidence is insufficient to warrant a formal recommendation.

Differences in hypersensitivity rates among GBCAs exist but are small, and the absolute risk of a reaction is extremely low. Therefore, the selection of a specific GBCA should be guided by factors such as cost, diagnostic need, and T1 relaxivity.

In patients with prior contrast-induced anaphylaxis, using an alternative imaging method that does not require contrast is preferred to minimize breakthrough reaction risk. If contrast is necessary, switch to a different agent and monitor the patient closely during and after administration. Premedication should not be used.

After stabilization of a patient with anaphylaxis, obtain serum tryptase 30–120 minutes after symptom onset to aid in confirming an immediate hypersensitivity reaction. Referral to an allergist should be considered if feasible.

In patients with a prior hypersensitivity reaction to nonvascular contrast agents, future administration—whether vascular or nonvascular—should involve switching to a different agent without premedication. Adverse events after nonvascular contrast are extremely rare and not well documented; thus, premedication is not supported.
Patients should not be required to fast before intravascular contrast administration, unless the examination itself demands it (e.g., CT or MR enterography).

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with a history of mild immediate hypersensitivity reaction to iodinated contrast media (e.g., limited urticaria, pruritus)
decision_rules: If the prior reaction was mild (isolated urticaria), consider no premedication or premedication with a second-generation antihistamine.
Contrast switching may further reduce risk but is not always necessary.
Avoid first-generation antihistamines due to side effects.
Corticosteroid premedication is not recommended due to lack of strong evidence and potential harms.

recommended_regimens.name: Second-generation antihistamine premedication
recommended_regimens.summary: Administer a second-generation oral antihistamine (e.g., cetirizine 10 mg) 1-2 hours prior to contrast administration. This may reduce breakthrough reactions from 16.6% to 10.7% (OR 0.569, 95% CI 0.443-0.731).
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Reduction in mild breakthrough reaction rate

recommended_regimens.name: No premedication (optional)
recommended_regimens.summary: In patients with isolated urticaria, some centers have abandoned premedication as there is no proven benefit with antihistamines.

alternative_regimens.name: Switch to a different low-osmolar ICM with a different side chain
alternative_regimens.summary: Switching the ICM agent reduces the risk of breakthrough reactions by 61% (risk ratio 0.39, 95% credible interval 0.24-0.58) and is an effective strategy, especially if premedication fails.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: When repeat reaction occurs despite premedication or if patient preference.

not_recommended.name: Corticosteroid premedication
not_recommended.reason: Evidence does not support efficacy; NNT to prevent one reaction of any severity is 69 (95% CI 39-304), and for severe reactions 569 (95% CI 389-1083). Potential harms include delayed hospital stay, fractures, infections.

not_recommended.name: First-generation antihistamines
not_recommended.reason: Lower safety and efficacy profile; CSACI recommends second/third generation antihistamines.

response_assessment.timepoint: During and up to 1 hour after contrast administration
response_assessment.method: Clinical monitoring for signs of hypersensitivity (urticaria, bronchospasm, hypotension)
response_assessment.interpretation: If breakthrough reaction occurs, treat per anaphylaxis guidelines.

supportive_care: Ensure availability of emergency anaphylaxis medications (epinephrine, antihistamines, IV fluids).
Patient education on recognizing and reporting symptoms.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: For mild reactions, antihistamine alone may suffice. Documentation of specific culprit agent is critical for future management.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with a history of moderate to severe immediate hypersensitivity reaction to ICM (e.g., diffuse urticaria, bronchospasm, anaphylaxis)
decision_rules: Contrast switching is the most effective strategy to reduce breakthrough reactions.
Select an ICM with a different side chain structure (see Table 1) to minimize cross-reactivity.
Premedication with antihistamines may be added but evidence is limited.
Corticosteroid premedication is not routinely recommended due to lack of strong efficacy and potential harms.
Consider allergy consultation and skin testing (skin prick, intradermal) 2-6 months after the reaction to guide choice.

If urgent imaging required and no time for testing, switch to a structurally different ICM and consider accelerated IV corticosteroid protocol (5-hour) as an alternative, though efficacy is uncertain.

recommended_regimens.name: Switch to a different low-osmolar ICM
recommended_regimens.summary: Switching to an ICM with a different chemical structure reduces the risk of recurrent immediate hypersensitivity; breakthrough reaction rates dropped from 27.7% (same ICM without premedication) to 2.9% (different ICM without premedication). Substitution with a structurally different agent had OR 0.51 (95% CI 0.37-0.69) for repeat reaction.
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Reduction in breakthrough reaction rate to approximately 3-8%

recommended_regimens.name: Second-generation antihistamine premedication (optional)
recommended_regimens.summary: May be added but evidence is limited; in one study, switching plus premedication did not show significant difference from switching alone.

alternative_regimens.name: Accelerated IV corticosteroid premedication (5-hour protocol) with antihistamine
alternative_regimens.summary: An accelerated 5-hour IV corticosteroid protocol was non-inferior to traditional 13-hour oral regimen in preventing breakthrough reactions (2.5% vs 2.1%), but neither prevented all moderate/severe reactions. May be considered when prolonged oral protocol is not feasible and rapid imaging needed.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: When urgent imaging is required and oral premedication cannot be completed.

not_recommended.name: Routine corticosteroid premedication (oral or IV) as sole strategy
not_recommended.reason: Insufficient evidence for efficacy; potential harms outweigh benefits. NNT to prevent severe reaction is 569 (95% CI 389-1083).

not_recommended.name: Re-using the same ICM agent without switching
not_recommended.reason: Higher breakthrough reaction rates (19% with premedication, 15% without).

not_recommended.name: First-generation antihistamines
not_recommended.reason: Higher side effect profile; not recommended by CSACI.

response_assessment.timepoint: During and for at least 30-60 minutes after contrast administration
response_assessment.method: Continuous monitoring for signs of anaphylaxis; consider serum tryptase measurement if reaction occurs
response_assessment.interpretation: Treat any breakthrough reaction immediately per anaphylaxis protocol.

supportive_care: Ensure immediate availability of emergency drugs and equipment (epinephrine auto-injector, IV access, oxygen).
Document the specific contrast agent and reaction details in the medical record and imaging report.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Allergy consultation is recommended for severe reactions (anaphylaxis) before re-exposure. Skin testing may identify safe alternatives.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with a history of immediate hypersensitivity reaction to gadolinium-based contrast agents (any severity)
decision_rules: Contrast switching is the most effective strategy to reduce breakthrough reactions.
Switch to a GBCA of a different class (e.g., from linear ionic to macrocyclic) and different molecular structure.
Premedication with antihistamines or corticosteroids is of uncertain benefit.
The incidence of HRs to GBCAs is very low overall.

recommended_regimens.name: Switch to a different GBCA (different class/molecular structure)
recommended_regimens.summary: Switching the GBCA reduced breakthrough reaction rates significantly: from 25.8% (same GBCA) to 6.9% (different GBCA) in one study. In another, switching with or without premedication resulted in a 3.7% breakthrough rate. Switching alone had OR 0.3 (95% CI 0.2-0.5).
recommended_regimens.key_outcomes: Breakthrough reaction rate approximately 3.7-6.9% with switching

alternative_regimens.name: Second-generation antihistamine premedication (if switching not possible or added precaution)
alternative_regimens.summary: May be considered, but evidence shows no significant difference between premedicated and non-premedicated groups when switching is done.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: When only one GBCA is available or patient refuses switching.

not_recommended.name: Corticosteroid premedication without switching
not_recommended.reason: No clear benefit; switching alone appears sufficient and avoids steroid risks.

not_recommended.name: Re-using the same GBCA
not_recommended.reason: Higher breakthrough reaction rates (19.0% with premedication, 31.4% without).

response_assessment.timepoint: During and for 30 minutes after GBCA injection
response_assessment.interpretation: Manage any breakthrough reaction as per anaphylaxis guidelines.

supportive_care: Document the culprit GBCA and reaction details in the health record.
treatment_pathways.special_considerations: For severe reactions, consider allergy evaluation. Skin testing is less sensitive for GBCA; provocation challenges may be considered under specialist supervision.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with a history of delayed hypersensitivity reactions to contrast media (ICM or GBCA), such as maculopapular exanthem
decision_rules: Premedication is not recommended for prevention of delayed HRs.
Contrast switching is the preferred strategy if re-exposure is necessary.
Allergy investigations (patch testing, delayed intradermal testing) can be considered to identify safe alternatives, but are not mandatory.
Corticosteroid premedication does not reliably prevent delayed reactions.

recommended_regimens.name: Switch to a different contrast agent (structurally different class)
recommended_regimens.summary: Use an alternate ICM or GBCA with a different chemical structure. Avoid the culprit agent. Premedication is not recommended.

not_recommended.name: Premedication with corticosteroids or antihistamines
not_recommended.reason: No evidence of efficacy for delayed reactions; may cause unnecessary side effects.

response_assessment.method: Patient education to report delayed skin eruptions; consider follow-up if needed

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Document the onset and nature of the index reaction to avoid premedication confusion. In severe delayed reactions (SJS/TEN, DRESS), avoid all contrast media if possible.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Patients with prior hypersensitivity reaction to intravascular contrast media who require non-vascular contrast (enteric, etc.)
decision_rules: The working group does not endorse premedication for non-vascular contrast media administration.
Adverse reactions to non-vascular contrast are very rare.
If the patient has a history of reaction to non-vascular contrast itself, consider switching the agent.

recommended_regimens.name: No premedication
recommended_regimens.summary: Administer non-vascular contrast without premedication. Risk of reaction is extremely low.

alternative_regimens.name: Switch non-vascular contrast agent if prior reaction to that specific agent
alternative_regimens.summary: Consider using a different non-vascular contrast medium (e.g., different iodine concentration or brand) if there is a documented reaction to the previous non-vascular agent.
alternative_regimens.conditions_for_use: Only if there is a known reaction to non-vascular contrast.

not_recommended.name: Premedication for non-vascular procedures
not_recommended.reason: No evidence to support its use; reactions are rare.

response_assessment.method: Standard post-procedure monitoring if any systemic absorption is expected

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: If the non-vascular contrast could be absorbed or leak into the circulation (e.g., during procedures), follow same precautions as intravascular administration.

treatment_pathways.patient_population: Pediatric patients (children) with a history of hypersensitivity reaction to contrast media (ICM or GBCA)
decision_rules: Pediatric patients have lower baseline HR rates than adults (adjusted OR 0.58 for ICM).
Management is similar to adults, with weight-adjusted doses.
Premedication with corticosteroids should be avoided in children due to risk of infections, behavioral changes, and fractures.
Contrast switching is preferred.

recommended_regimens.name: Switch to a different contrast agent (weight-appropriate dose)
recommended_regimens.summary: Use an alternative ICM or GBCA as per adult guidelines. Dose based on weight.

recommended_regimens.name: Second-generation antihistamine premedication (if deemed necessary)
recommended_regimens.summary: If premedication is considered, use a second-generation antihistamine at pediatric weight-based dosing.

not_recommended.name: Corticosteroid premedication in children
not_recommended.reason: Short-course oral corticosteroids in children are associated with vomiting, behavioral changes, sleep disturbance, and infections; risk of fracture (OR 1.17).

response_assessment.method: Monitoring appropriate for pediatric patients; have pediatric emergency equipment
response_assessment.interpretation: Manage any reaction per pediatric anaphylaxis guidelines.

treatment_pathways.special_considerations: Fasting prior to contrast is not recommended in children unless specifically required for the procedure.

artifacts.title: Types of Iodinated Contrast Media and Common Side Chain Structures
artifacts.summary: Categorizes iodinated contrast media available in Canada based on the presence of two side chain structures, facilitating the selection of agents with differing molecular profiles.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Guides contrast switching by identifying agents with distinct side chains, thereby reducing the risk of breakthrough hypersensitivity reactions due to shared epitopes.

artifacts.title: Categories of Gadolinium-Based Contrast Agents
artifacts.summary: Lists gadolinium-based contrast agents by molecular structure (linear versus macrocyclic) and charge (ionic versus nonionic). Agents marked with an asterisk transiently bind plasma proteins.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: The risk of hypersensitivity reactions varies by GBCA structure; macrocyclic and ionic agents are associated with higher reaction rates, and protein binding is an independent risk factor.

Prophylaxis may be of some benefit, though there is no specific recommendation. Consider alternate contrast agent.
Prophylaxis (steroids, antihistamines) is recommended combined with changing the class of agent.

If severe, avoid contrast if possible. If impossible, base alternate choice on allergy testing if favourable risk-benefit ratio.
Avoid use of contrast if possible. If contrast to be used, use alternate agent with prophylaxis, if testing previously unavailable.
SP/ID testing with trigger ICM and alternates. Consider IV DPT challenge to alternate media if needed.

All patients with non-severe reactions should use alternate ICM if urgent, or complete testing if time allows. If previously investigated, use alternate contrast choice. Prophylaxis, in general, not recommended, but may be considered if high risk individuals with severe HR's.

artifacts.summary: Comparison of recommendations from various international guidelines regarding prevention and investigation of acute and delayed hypersensitivity reactions to iodinated contrast media.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Highlights the lack of consensus and evolving evidence, guiding clinicians to adopt practices such as contrast switching over standard premedication protocols.

artifacts.title: Figure 1: Hypersensitivity reaction to LOCM or GBCA
artifacts.description: Step 1: Patient has a history of hypersensitivity reaction to a specific low-osmolality contrast medium (LOCM) or gadolinium-based contrast agent (GBCA). Step 2: Switch to a chemically different contrast agent. Step 3: If no breakthrough reaction occurs, proceed with routine monitoring. Step 4: If a mild or moderate breakthrough reaction occurs after switching, administer a third, different contrast agent. Step 5: If a severe breakthrough reaction occurs, consider an alternative imaging modality or allergy consultation.
artifacts.summary: Algorithm for managing patients with a prior hypersensitivity reaction to a known contrast agent, emphasizing contrast switching as the primary preventive measure.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Provides a structured approach to minimize risk of recurrent reactions, reducing reliance on premedication and guiding appropriate use of alternative agents.

artifacts.title: Figure 2: Hypersensitivity reaction to ICM unknown agent
artifacts.description: Step 1: Patient has a history of hypersensitivity reaction to iodinated contrast media (ICM) but the offending agent is unknown. Step 2: Determine if the reaction occurred before or after the year 2000. Step 3a: If before 2000, the agent was likely not a low-osmolality contrast media (LOCM); administer LOCM without premedication. Step 3b: If on or after 2000 and the reaction was severe (acute or delayed), consider an alternative imaging modality; if contrast is essential, consider allergy referral; premedication is not recommended. Step 3c: If on or after 2000 and the reaction was mild or moderate, consider premedication with second-generation antihistamines and monitor closely.
artifacts.summary: Decision tree for patients with an uncertain history of ICM hypersensitivity, using the date and severity of the index reaction to guide management.
artifacts.clinical_relevance: Helps clinicians safely manage patients when the culprit contrast agent cannot be identified, balancing the need for contrast-enhanced imaging with the risk of recurrence.

artifacts.clinical_relevance: Skin prick and intradermal testing have limited sensitivity; drug provocation testing remains the gold standard but is logistically challenging. These tests may be considered in select cases but are not routinely recommended over contrast switching.
